questions.title: The smallest unit of an antigen that is capable of binding with antibodies is:
questions.question: The smallest unit of an antigen that is capable of binding with antibodies is:

options.A: Adjuvant

explanations.A: Incorrect. An adjuvant is a substance that boosts an immune response to an accompanying antigen; it is not itself the antibody-binding unit of an antigen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hapten is a small molecule that cannot provoke an antibody response alone unless bound to a carrier protein — a separate concept from the antigen-binding unit itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The paratope is the antigen-binding site on the antibody, the complementary partner to the epitope, not a unit of the antigen.
explanations.D: Correct. The epitope (also called the antigenic determinant) is the smallest structural unit of an antigen that is specifically recognised and bound by an antibody or a T-cell receptor. A single antigen molecule, especially a large protein, typically carries multiple epitopes, and it is the epitope — not the whole antigen molecule — that defines antibody specificity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A tolerogen is a form of antigen that induces immunological tolerance rather than a response; it is not the antibody-binding unit.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the epitope as the smallest antibody-binding unit of an antigen.

questions.title: Which of the following criteria should be fulfilled for a substance to be antigenic?
questions.question: Which of the following criteria should be fulfilled for a substance to be antigenic?

options.A: Low molecular weight

explanations.A: Incorrect. Low molecular weight actually works against immunogenicity — small molecules (haptens) generally cannot provoke a response alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Structural simplicity works against, not for, antigenicity; a repetitive, simple structure is poorly immunogenic.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Having only one antigenic determinant is not a criterion for antigenicity — larger, more complex antigens typically carry multiple epitopes and are more immunogenic, not fewer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Resistance to degradation is not by itself a criterion for antigenicity; it can affect persistence but does not define what makes a substance antigenic.
explanations.E: Correct. Chemical complexity — a varied, non-repetitive composition of amino acids or sugars — is a genuine criterion for antigenicity, working alongside sufficient size and foreignness to the host. A structurally simple, uniform molecule is generally a poor antigen even if it is otherwise large.

questions.learning_objective: Identify chemical complexity as a genuine criterion for antigenicity.

questions.title: MHC class II on APCs is recognized by T cell through:
questions.question: MHC class II on APCs is recognized by T cell through:

options.A: CD8

explanations.A: Incorrect. CD8 is the co-receptor for MHC class I, not class II.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. The T-cell receptor is necessary for MHC class II recognition, but on its own it is not sufficient — CD4 is also required, which is why 'b&c' rather than TCR alone is the complete answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. CD4 stabilises and strengthens the interaction with MHC class II, but recognition also requires the TCR itself, so CD4 alone is not the full answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CD3 is the signal-transducing complex associated with the TCR, not the molecule that binds MHC class II.
explanations.E: Correct. MHC class II on an antigen-presenting cell is recognised by a T cell through the combination of its TCR (binding the peptide-MHC complex) and its CD4 co-receptor (binding a separate site on MHC class II). This is the class-II mirror of class I's TCR+CD8 pairing, and is why MHC class II presents specifically to CD4+ T helper cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that MHC class II is recognised through the combination of TCR and CD4.

questions.title: MHC restriction:
questions.question: MHC restriction:

options.A: Is a character of MQ & B cells
options.B: Involves CD3 molecule on T cells
options.C: Peptide Ags are recognized by T cell only in association with self MHC

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Macrophages and B cells are professional antigen-presenting cells that display MHC-bound peptide, but MHC restriction is fundamentally a property of how T cells recognise antigen, which is why this alone is not the complete picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. CD3 is genuinely involved, as the signal-transducing complex accompanying the TCR during MHC-restricted recognition, but this alone omits the core defining fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone (though this IS the core defining statement). T cells recognise processed peptide antigen only when it is presented in association with a self MHC molecule — this is what "MHC restriction" means — but the question also credits the other true statements as part of the full picture.
explanations.D: Correct. MHC restriction is the phenomenon in which a T cell recognises peptide antigen only when presented in the context of a self MHC molecule. Antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and B cells display this MHC-peptide combination, and the T cell's CD3 complex accompanies the TCR during the recognition event — so a, b and c are all genuinely part of MHC restriction, making 'all of the above' correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that MHC restriction means a T cell recognises peptide antigen only in association with self MHC.

questions.title: Class I MHC proteins:
questions.question: Class I MHC proteins:

options.A: Present Ag to CD4 helper T cell
options.B: Encoded by HLA DP, DQ, DR loci
options.D: Heterodimers composed of an alpha chain & β2 microglobulin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Class I MHC presents to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, not CD4+ helper T cells — that pairing belongs to class II.
explanations.B: Incorrect. HLA-DP, -DQ and -DR are the class II loci; class I is encoded by HLA-A, -B and -C.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mature red blood cells lack MHC molecules entirely, including class I, since they have no nucleus and shed their surface MHC during maturation.
explanations.D: Correct. Class I MHC proteins are heterodimers composed of a polymorphic alpha (heavy) chain, encoded by HLA-A, -B or -C, non-covalently associated with the invariant beta-2 microglobulin light chain. Beta-2 microglobulin does not itself carry the peptide-binding groove, but it is required for the alpha chain to fold correctly and reach the cell surface. Without it, class I expression is lost, which is exactly why beta-2 microglobulin deficiency causes a class-I-deficient immunodeficiency.

questions.learning_objective: State that class I MHC proteins are alpha-chain/beta-2-microglobulin heterodimers.

questions.title: MHC class I & class II Ag receptors are located on:
questions.question: MHC class I & class II Ag receptors are located on:

options.A: T cells

explanations.A: Incorrect per the printed key. Read strictly as "the T-cell receptor that recognises MHC-bound peptide", this would point to T cells — but the bank's own printed key selects antigen-presenting cells instead, read as "where the MHC molecules that carry antigen are found".
explanations.B: Incorrect. B cells are one specific type of antigen-presenting cell (for class II), but the printed key answer names the broader category, not B cells specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. NK cells are not the population this stem or its printed key are pointing to.
explanations.D: Correct as printed. This bank's own answer key selects antigen-presenting cells for this stem. The stem is genuinely ambiguous — "Ag receptor" more naturally suggests the T-cell receptor (found on T cells), but the printed key reads it as asking where the MHC molecules bearing antigen are displayed, which is the antigen-presenting cell for class II (and, more broadly, nearly all nucleated cells for class I). Kept as printed rather than silently corrected.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise this bank's printed-key reading of MHC "Ag receptor" location as antigen-presenting cells.

field_notes.hegazy: Chapter 3 Q6, key = d (printed-key oddity, ambiguous stem)

questions.author_notes: Printed key kept as-is despite the stem's ambiguity ("Ag receptor" could mean TCR-on-T-cells or MHC-molecule-location); see CON-IMM-F6417EBDCB51D8 field_notes for the reasoning.

questions.title: Class I MHC:
questions.question: Class I MHC:

options.A: Able to carry an Ag fragment
options.B: Recognized by TCR protein on T cell
options.C: Combination with Ag fragment to mark a cell for killing by cytotoxic T cell

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Class I MHC genuinely does carry a processed peptide (antigen) fragment in its groove, but this is only part of the full picture the question credits.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. The TCR, together with CD8, does recognise class I MHC-peptide complexes, but this alone omits the other true statements.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. Marking an infected or abnormal cell for cytotoxic T-cell killing is indeed what the class-I-peptide complex achieves, but again this is only one part of the complete answer.
explanations.D: Correct. Class I MHC binds and displays a processed peptide fragment in its groove; this peptide-MHC complex is recognised by the TCR (together with CD8) on a cytotoxic T cell; and this recognition event marks the presenting cell for killing if the peptide is foreign (viral or tumour-derived). All three statements describe one continuous mechanism, so 'all of the above' is correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that class I MHC carries a peptide fragment recognised by TCR+CD8, marking the cell for cytotoxic T-cell killing.

questions.title: Which statement about antigen epitope is true?
questions.question: Which statement about antigen epitope is true?

options.A: An epitope may be shared between 2 different antigens
options.B: A protein molecule usually contains multiple epitopes
options.C: Some epitopes are more immunogenic than others

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Epitope sharing between different antigens genuinely occurs (this underlies cross-reactivity), but it is only one of the true statements listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. A protein antigen usually does carry multiple distinct epitopes, but again this is only part of the full picture.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. Not every epitope on an antigen is equally immunogenic — some are immunodominant and provoke a stronger response than others — but this alone omits the other true statements.
explanations.D: Correct. All three statements are true. An epitope can be structurally shared between two different antigens, which is the molecular basis of antibody cross-reactivity. A typical protein antigen also carries multiple distinct epitopes, which is part of why larger, more complex molecules tend to be more immunogenic. And epitopes are not all equally immunogenic — some are immunodominant and provoke a stronger response than the others on the same molecule.

questions.learning_objective: State that a protein antigen typically carries multiple epitopes of unequal immunogenicity, which can be shared between different antigens.

questions.title: The following statement best describes haptens:
questions.question: The following statement best describes haptens:

options.A: Haptens activate B cells
options.C: Haptens don't react with specific Ab

explanations.A: Incorrect. A hapten alone cannot activate B cells or provoke an antibody response; it must first be conjugated to a carrier protein to become immunogenic.
explanations.B: Correct. Penicillin is a classic clinical example of a hapten. On its own, penicillin is too small to provoke an immune response, but it can covalently attach to host carrier proteins in vivo. That hapten-carrier conjugate is what becomes immunogenic and can trigger antibody responses, which is the mechanism behind penicillin allergy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A hapten does react with (and can be bound by) specific antibody once an immune response to the hapten-carrier conjugate has been raised; what it cannot do alone is provoke that response in the first place.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Binding MHC is not the defining feature of a hapten; a hapten's defining feature is its need for a carrier protein to become immunogenic.

questions.learning_objective: Identify penicillin as a clinical example of a hapten.

questions.title: Sites on the Ag which will elicit immune response & react with antibodies:
questions.question: Sites on the Ag which will elicit immune response & react with antibodies:

options.A: Agglutinins

explanations.A: Incorrect. Agglutinins are the antibodies that cause clumping of particulate antigen, not the antigen's own binding sites.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Agglutinogens are the particulate antigens themselves (e.g. on red cells) that are agglutinated by antibody, not the specific binding sites on them.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Precipitin describes an antibody that forms a visible precipitate with soluble antigen, again a reagent term rather than the antigen's binding site.
explanations.D: Correct. Antigenic determinants — a synonym for epitopes — are the specific sites on an antigen molecule that elicit an immune response and are the sites antibodies actually bind. This is the same underlying fact as "epitope is the smallest antibody-binding unit" tested elsewhere in this chapter, restated with the alternative term.

questions.learning_objective: Identify "antigenic determinants" as the term for the sites on an antigen that elicit response and bind antibody (i.e. epitopes).

questions.title: Antigen entering the body in a subcutaneous injection activates its specific lymphocytes in:
questions.question: Antigen entering the body in a subcutaneous injection activates its specific lymphocytes in:

options.A: Blood circulation

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood circulation is where the spleen, not lymph nodes, filters and encounters blood-borne antigen; a subcutaneous antigen does not reach the blood first.
explanations.B: Correct. Antigen entering subcutaneously drains via lymphatic vessels into the nearest (draining) lymph node. There, naive lymphocytes, the antigen itself and antigen-presenting cells converge in one confined space, which is what allows a rare antigen-specific lymphocyte to actually find its antigen and become activated. This is the activation site, not the bloodstream, the bone marrow, or the skin injection site itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The skin is the site of entry, not the site of lymphocyte activation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spleen filters blood-borne antigen; a subcutaneously injected antigen reaches the draining lymph node via lymphatics, not the spleen via blood.

questions.learning_objective: State that a subcutaneously injected antigen activates lymphocytes in the draining lymph node.

questions.title: Innate & acquired immunity differ in:
questions.question: Innate & acquired immunity differ in:

options.A: Period required before it gets into action

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Innate immunity acts within minutes to hours while acquired immunity takes days, a genuine difference, but only one of several the question lists.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Innate immunity responds non-specifically while acquired immunity is antigen-specific, but this too is only part of the full answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. Only acquired immunity produces memory cells for a faster, stronger response on re-exposure; innate immunity does not, but again this is only one difference among several.
explanations.D: Incorrect alone. The cell types involved differ (phagocytes and NK cells for innate; T and B lymphocytes for acquired), but this too is just one of the listed differences.
explanations.E: Correct. Innate and acquired immunity differ across all of these dimensions at once. Innate immunity is rapid, non-specific, generates no memory, and uses phagocytes and NK cells as its main cellular components. Acquired immunity, by contrast, is slower to develop, highly antigen-specific, generates memory for stronger repeat responses, and uses T and B lymphocytes as its cellular components. Because each of the four listed features genuinely differs between the two systems, 'all of the above' is the complete answer.

questions.learning_objective: State the multiple dimensions along which innate and acquired immunity differ (timing, specificity, memory, cell types).

questions.title: T cell receptors, when co-expressed with CD8 molecules, are restricted to recognizing and binding peptide fragments associated with:
questions.question: T cell receptors, when co-expressed with CD8 molecules, are restricted to recognizing and binding peptide fragments associated with:

options.A: CD3 molecules

explanations.A: Incorrect. CD3 is the signal-transducing complex that accompanies the TCR regardless of CD4/CD8 co-receptor status; it is not the restriction element itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CD4, not CD8, is co-expressed with TCRs restricted to MHC class II.
explanations.C: Correct. A TCR co-expressed with the CD8 co-receptor is restricted to recognising peptide presented by MHC class I. CD8 binds a conserved region of the class I molecule while the TCR itself reads the specific peptide sitting in its groove, and together the two proteins are what make this the defining pairing of the cytotoxic T-cell lineage. This is why CD8+ T cells specifically target virally infected or tumour cells displaying foreign peptide on class I.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MHC class II restriction pairs with CD4, not CD8.

questions.learning_objective: State that CD8-co-expressing TCRs are restricted to MHC class I.

questions.title: Codominant expression of MHC genes leads to:
questions.question: Codominant expression of MHC genes leads to:

options.A: High polymorphism of MHC genes in humans
options.C: Expression of 12 different HLA proteins on cell surface

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Codominant expression is part of why MHC genes are so polymorphic across the population, but this bank keys the more specific numerical consequence (c), not this broader statement, as the answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. MHC mismatch (a consequence of this diversity) does drive transplant rejection, but the printed key selects the specific 12-protein consequence over this broader downstream effect.
explanations.C: Correct as printed. Codominant expression means both alleles at every classical MHC locus are expressed simultaneously on the cell surface, rather than one allele being silenced. With two alleles at each of the six classical class I and class II loci, a single (heterozygous) cell can therefore display up to 12 distinct HLA proteins at once. This is the specific numerical consequence the bank's key selects for this stem.
explanations.D: Incorrect per the printed key, even though (a) and (b) are also true consequences of MHC diversity — this bank's key selects the specific numerical fact (c) rather than 'all of the above'.

questions.learning_objective: State that codominant expression of two alleles at each of six MHC loci allows up to 12 distinct HLA proteins per cell.

field_notes.hegazy: Chapter 3 Q14, key = c (printed key selects the specific 12-protein fact over 'all of the above')

questions.title: A mother doesn't reject a fetus with different MHC alleles due to:
questions.question: A mother doesn't reject a fetus with different MHC alleles due to:

options.A: Absence of MHC I on RBCs
options.B: Low expression of MHC I on sperms & trophoblasts
options.C: Absence of MHC II on sperms & trophoblasts

explanations.A: Incorrect. Absence of MHC on red blood cells is real but unrelated to maternal-fetal tolerance — RBCs are not the fetal-maternal interface.
explanations.B: Correct. MHC class I expression on sperm and on the trophoblast layer, which forms the fetal-maternal interface, is low. This sharply limits the paternal alloantigen that the mother's immune system is actually exposed to. Because the mother's T cells rarely encounter foreign class I on the cells that matter, the genetically mismatched fetus is not rejected.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The protective mechanism is specifically about MHC class I, not class II, expression at the sperm/trophoblast interface.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only the low-MHC-I-expression fact (b) is correct; the RBC and class II statements are not accurate descriptions of the maternal-fetal tolerance mechanism, so 'all of the above' overstates it.

questions.learning_objective: State that low MHC class I expression on sperm and trophoblast cells explains maternal-fetal tolerance of MHC mismatch.

questions.title: DR molecules are present on:
questions.question: DR molecules are present on:

options.A: Ag presenting cells

explanations.A: Correct. HLA-DR molecules are MHC class II gene products. Like other class II molecules, they are expressed constitutively on professional antigen-presenting cells — dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells — rather than broadly across all nucleated cells the way class I is. This restricted distribution is exactly what confines class II antigen presentation to the cells whose job is presenting antigen to CD4+ T helper cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DR (class II) is not constitutively expressed on virally infected cells as such; that broader expression pattern belongs to class I.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tumour cells do not constitutively express class II DR molecules; class II expression is restricted to professional APCs (and some activated non-APC cells under inflammatory conditions, not a general rule).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since DR expression is restricted to antigen-presenting cells rather than found on VICs or tumour cells generally, 'all of the above' overstates its distribution.

questions.learning_objective: State that DR (MHC class II) molecules are expressed on antigen-presenting cells.

questions.title: Each person has:
questions.question: Each person has:

options.A: 2 sets of MHC genes
options.B: 2 alleles of each of 6 MHC genes

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. It is true each person inherits two sets of MHC genes, one from each parent, but this is only one of the true statements listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. There are genuinely two alleles at each of the six classical MHC loci, but this alone is not the complete answer credited here.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. A person expresses up to six distinct class I proteins (three loci x two alleles, when heterozygous), which is true but again only part of the full picture.
explanations.D: Correct. All three statements describe the same underlying MHC genetics from different angles. Each person inherits two parental sets of MHC genes, giving two alleles at each of the six classical loci. For class I alone, this heterozygosity means up to six distinct class I proteins (three loci, two alleles each) can be displayed on the cell surface at once.

questions.learning_objective: State the structure of MHC gene inheritance: two parental gene sets, two alleles per locus, multiple class I proteins expressed.

questions.title: How can you define Antigen:
questions.question: How can you define Antigen:

options.A: Agent capable of binding specifically to component of immune response when introduced into the body
options.B: Any substance stimulates the production of heterophile antibodies
options.C: Inherited self protein present only on the surface of nucleated cells
options.D: Soluble proteins produced by cells in response to microbes

explanations.A: Correct. An antigen is generally defined as any agent capable of binding specifically to a component of the immune response — an antibody or a T-cell receptor — once it enters the body. This is the broad, general definition, distinct from the narrower related terms in the other options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes a heterophile antigen specifically (one that provokes cross-reactive antibodies against unrelated species), a narrower term than "antigen" itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes an inherited self (MHC) protein, a specific class of self molecule, not the general definition of antigen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes cytokines or other microbe-induced soluble proteins, not the general definition of antigen.

questions.learning_objective: State the general definition of an antigen as an agent that specifically binds a component of the immune response.

questions.title: A low molecular weight substance can't induce immune response unless conjugated to a carrier molecule; it is called:
questions.question: A low molecular weight substance can't induce immune response unless conjugated to a carrier molecule; it is called:

options.A: Antigen

explanations.A: Incorrect. A full antigen does not need carrier conjugation to be immunogenic on its own; this describes the opposite of an antigen's usual behaviour.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An antigen epitope is the binding site on an antigen, not a substance defined by its need for a carrier.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the definition of a hapten: a small, low-molecular-weight molecule that cannot provoke an antibody response by itself. Once it becomes covalently bound to a larger carrier protein, however, the hapten-carrier conjugate becomes immunogenic and can raise an antibody response. Penicillin, tested elsewhere in this chapter, is the clinical example of exactly this fact.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A heterophil antigen is a shared antigen that provokes cross-reactive antibodies against an unrelated species, a different concept from a hapten's carrier requirement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An immunogen is, by definition, something that CAN provoke an immune response on its own — the opposite of the carrier-dependent substance described here.

questions.learning_objective: State that a low-molecular-weight substance needing carrier conjugation to become immunogenic is a hapten.

questions.title: What is the principle function of class I MHC molecules?
questions.question: What is the principle function of class I MHC molecules?

options.A: They display peptide Ags for B cells
options.B: They display peptide Ags for CD4 molecules on T helper cells
options.C: They display peptide Ags for CD8 molecules on T cytotoxic cells
options.D: They help endocytosis by phagocytic cells
options.E: They recognize microbes by Pathogen associated molecular patterns

explanations.A: Incorrect. B cells recognise native, unprocessed antigen through their B-cell receptor, not processed peptide displayed on MHC class I.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Displaying peptide for CD4 T helper cells is the function of MHC class II, not class I.
explanations.C: Correct. The principal function of class I MHC molecules is to display processed peptide antigen, typically derived from intracellular or cytosolic proteins, in the groove between its alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains. This peptide-class-I complex is what CD8 molecules on cytotoxic T cells recognise. That recognition event is exactly the mechanism that lets cytotoxic T cells identify and kill virally infected or tumour cells from the inside out.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Assisting phagocytic endocytosis is not an MHC function; MHC molecules present already-processed peptide, they do not drive the uptake step.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Recognising PAMPs is the role of pattern recognition receptors (e.g. Toll-like receptors) in innate immunity, not of MHC class I.

questions.learning_objective: State that the principal function of MHC class I is presenting peptide antigen to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.

questions.title: What is the principle function of class II MHC molecules?
questions.question: What is the principle function of class II MHC molecules?

options.A: They display peptide Ags for B cells
options.B: They display peptide Ags for CD4 molecules on T helper cells
options.C: They display peptide Ags for CD8 molecules on T cytotoxic cells
options.D: Their Ag binding site lies between al & a2 domains
options.E: They recognize microbes by Pathogen associated molecular patterns

explanations.A: Incorrect. B cells recognise native antigen through their own receptor, not peptide displayed to them by MHC class II.
explanations.B: Correct. The principal function of class II MHC molecules is to display processed peptide antigen, typically derived from extracellular or endocytosed proteins, for recognition by CD4 molecules on T helper cells. This is the mechanism underlying CD4+ T-cell activation. Downstream of that activation, helper T cells go on to license B cells for antibody production and macrophages for enhanced microbial killing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Displaying peptide for CD8 cytotoxic T cells is the function of class I MHC, not class II.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The class I (not class II) antigen-binding groove is formed between the alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains; class II's groove instead forms between one alpha and one beta domain.
explanations.E: Incorrect. PAMP recognition is an innate pattern-recognition-receptor function, not a role of MHC class II.

questions.learning_objective: State that the principal function of MHC class II is presenting peptide antigen to CD4+ T helper cells.

questions.title: Linkage of a disease to an HLA allele means that:
questions.question: Linkage of a disease to an HLA allele means that:

options.A: Everyone with that allele will eventually get the disease
options.B: People with that allele have a higher risk for the disease
options.C: MHC protein encoded by that allele is defective
options.D: The allele will eventually disappear from the population
options.E: Non of the above is true

explanations.A: Incorrect. An HLA-disease association is a risk modifier, not a deterministic guarantee — most carriers of a disease-linked allele never develop the disease.
explanations.B: Correct. Linkage of a disease to a particular HLA allele means that people carrying that allele have a statistically higher risk of developing the disease compared with the general population. It is an association derived from population studies, not a deterministic guarantee. Most carriers of even a strongly disease-linked allele, such as HLA-B27 and ankylosing spondylitis, never actually develop the disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The MHC protein encoded by a disease-linked allele is not inherently defective; the allele's structure may influence immune recognition patterns in ways that raise disease risk without the protein being non-functional.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A disease-linked allele is not expected to simply disappear from the population; many disease-associated HLA alleles persist because they also confer other advantages (e.g. resistance to certain infections).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option B is a true and complete description of what an HLA-disease linkage means, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that an HLA-disease linkage confers increased relative risk, not certainty, of disease.
